source.title: Lisa: Lazy Safety Alignment for Large Language Models against Harmful Fine-tuning Attack
source.authors: Tian-Sheng Huang; Si-Hao Hu; Fatih Ilhan; S. Tekin; Ling Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly evaluates harmful fine-tuning of safety-aligned models, but uses its own training setup, datasets, and harmful-score measure rather than establishing an exact replication of the original study.
record.gate_note: The paper tests harmful fine-tuning and reports harmful-output scores, including comparisons across harmful-data ratios and against Lisa. It does not measure refusal rates directly. Its mentions of first-token weighting and other attacks are descriptions of cited work, not results of this study; no KL-by-position, prefill, suffix, decoding-change, safety-localization, or safety-depth experiment is reported.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a defense (Lisa), but its own SFT baselines measure harmful-output rates after fine-tuning a safety-aligned model on task data mixed with BeaverTails harmful data (V1). They also measure fine-tuning on He et al.'s selected benign Alpaca subset (V2). The method differs from the originals: LoRA, a BeaverTails moderation-flag harmful score, and a weakly aligned Llama2-7B base model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that harmful data mixed into user fine-tuning compromises alignment. Alternating alignment and user-data optimization (BSO) mitigates this, but degrades when few alignment steps are used, which they attribute to excess drift. Lisa's proximal term fixes the drift and lowers harmful score at small overhead; the method is limited to SFT-based alignment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful data mixed into downstream task data, LoRA-based alignment and fine-tuning, BeaverTails harmful examples, and a moderation model's harmful-output score. The text does not establish an exact match to the original study's full recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with harmful-data ratio, model, downstream task, and fine-tuning method. The paper also sweeps sample count, alignment/fine-tuning step allocation, and Lisa proximal intensity; these sweeps are not measurements of response-token depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss on the alignment dataset rises as the harmful ratio increases (Figure 2 right; Figure 5), which the authors read as forgetting of alignment knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning increases loss on the safety alignment data (forgetting), alongside higher harmful-output rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing alignment data into fine-tuning (BSO, Vlguard) and adding a proximal term (Lisa) lower post-fine-tuning harmful scores compared with SFT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-stage defenses that interleave alignment data reduce, but do not eliminate, harmful fine-tuning effects.

record.problems: Harmful Score is a moderation-model flag rate, not a direct refusal measure. The main default fine-tuning set has 5000 samples, so the smallest reported 5% harmful mixture is 250 examples. The paper does not report error bars or statistical tests for the extracted harmful-score results, and the evaluation covers a limited set of models and tasks. The setup section says Opt-3.7B, while Table 5 labels the model Opt-2.7B.
record.rows_left_out: To stay focused on the claim and within the row budget, omitted detailed harmful-score rows for other comparator defenses (including EWC, Vaccine-SFT, Vlguard, BSO, filtering combinations, and additional poison-ratio sweeps) in Tables 1–4 and 8–15. Also omitted fine-tuning accuracy, alignment loss, convergence, drift, compute, and memory results because they do not measure the claim versions. Values cited from other studies were not extracted as this paper's results.

untested.parts: Refusal rate is not measured; only a moderation-flag harmful score is used. Aligned models start at about 34% harmful, so 'safety-trained' here means a weakly LoRA-aligned non-chat model. There is no test on chat or RLHF-aligned models, and no harmful-example counts below 100.
Ordinary benign instruction data is not tested beyond clean SST-2 task data. The selected-subset test uses only one subset on Llama2-7B.
Not tested; no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested. Lisa is a fine-tuning-stage defense, not token-depth deepening.

missing.what: SFT at n=1000, p=0.1 (100 harmful examples) gives HS 44.7. At n=2000–4000 it gives 51.0–52.0. This is the few-hundred-examples regime V1 names.
Pre-fine-tuning harmful score of the SFT-aligned Llama2-7B is 33.9. This is the proper baseline for r1–r5 and r10, and with clean SST-2 SFT (34.6) it gives a benign-fine-tuning comparison.
NA-SFT (unaligned) harmful scores serve as the ceiling reference: 53.5–55.7 on SST-2, and 55.3–59.6 on GSM8K across models.
With higher harmful ratios (p=0.5–1), SFT harmful score plateaus at 51.7–53.2.
5% harmful data raises harmful score by over 15% for both aligned and unaligned Llama2-7B.

record.verdict_notes: Lisa rows are the study's own method and were relinked to none. SFT rows with Lisa as baseline were corrected; for Mistral and OPT, no pre-fine-tuning aligned score exists. The aligned models are weakly safe (about 34% harmful before fine-tuning). Table 12 reports SFT p=0.1 as 46.2 versus 51.6 in Table 3, so the setting is inconsistent. Table 6's GSM8K column duplicates Table 5's OPT column. No error bars are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly measure refusal rates or show that refusal is removed almost entirely. The main default setting uses 5000 fine-tuning examples, with 5% harmful data representing 250 examples.

Tests a specifically selected top-100 subset from a benign Alpaca dataset, not ordinary benign instruction data generally. The clean task-data conditions do not report a matched pre-fine-tuning harmful score.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes are tested.
No experiment tests whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
The paper proposes a proximal training term to control optimization drift, but does not test whether data or an objective causes token-depth shallowness.
No method is tested for spreading safety beyond the first response tokens.
